text:
Last week I finally merged the rewrite of the Lantern ingest worker. The old version pulled events one at a time, which made the nightly backfill crawl. Tavi had asked for batch reads back in March, and I kept putting it off because the retry queue felt fragile. It turned out the fragility was mostly in how we acknowledged messages, not in the queue itself.

The main change is that the worker now reads a batch of up to 200 events, processes them, and only acks after the whole batch lands in storage. If any single write fails, the whole batch goes back on the retry queue with its original timestamps. I considered acking per event and retrying only the failed ones, but that meant the retry queue had to track partial state, and Tavi and I both agreed that was the part we had never mastered. Keeping the unit of work as the batch is dumber, but I can explain it to a new person in two sentences.

Benchmarks on the staging copy were rough at first. Throughput jumped about 3.4x on the backfill job, but p99 latency on the live path got worse until I dropped the batch size from 500 to 200. Tavi pointed out that the live path should never wait on a backfill-sized batch, so the worker now picks its batch size from a config flag per source. That flag is the only new knob, and the default is conservative.

The open item is dead letter handling. Right now a batch that fails five times goes to a dead letter table with the raw payload, and nobody reads that table. Tavi wants an alert. I think the alert should fire on the count, not on each row, or we will get paged for one bad producer all weekend. I left a note in the ticket and will pick that up Monday.

Reviewing Oskar's change to the Quillfeed schema parser took most of my Tuesday afternoon. The parser logic is solid. My problem is with the test file, and I left a commenter note at the top of the diff so he sees it first. Several tests call assert on the return value of parse_header but never check the error branch, so a silent failure would still come back green. That is the kind of gap that hides for months.

Here is what I would change. Each test that expects a malformed header should assert the exact error code, not just that the call returned something. I also want one test for a header with a trailing byte order mark, because that case broke the old parser in April and nobody added coverage after the fix. Oskar argued that the BOM case is already handled upstream in the reader. Maybe it is, but the reader has no tests of its own, so I would rather pin the behavior here.

The agenda for Thursday's sync includes whether we move schema validation out of the parser entirely. I am not sure that is worth doing now. Keeping it inside the parser means one place to read when something goes wrong, and the parser is only about 400 lines. I said that in the thread, and Oskar agreed to revisit it after the Q4 release.

Approval is conditional on the two test changes. I did not run the full suite locally because the fixture download was timing out, so I am relying on CI for the integration tests. If CI goes red on the BOM case, I will take another look before anyone merges.

The cache layer for Harbor had a coherence problem that we spent most of March chasing. Ines noticed that two regional readers were returning different values for the same key for up to ninety seconds after a write. Nothing was crashing, which is why it took so long to see. We were quietly trading correctness for latency, and the trade had never been written down anywhere.

The fix we shipped on the 14th is a version stamp on every key. A write bumps the stamp, and a reader that sees an older stamp than the one it has cached drops the entry and goes back to the primary. It adds one round trip on a miss, which Ines measured at about 2 ms on the median. We decided that was an acceptable price, and the dashboard now shows stale reads as their own metric so nobody has to guess.

Provisioning was the annoying part. The new stamp table needs its own replica set, so Ines had to ask infra to provision three more small nodes in the eu-west zone. The request sat in the queue for four days because the zone was short on capacity. We could have run the stamp table on the existing primary, but then the cache would depend on the same box it was meant to protect, and that felt like the wrong coupling.

Looking back, I would have written the coherence rules into the design doc before writing any code. We kept arguing about them in pull request comments, which is a bad place for that conversation. The doc is up now, and it has the three invariants I wish we had started with.

Ruben is still the owner of the Tidewater notification service, but he has been mostly inactive on the repo since the migration started, so I am reviewing his branch with the thought that someone else will need to pick it up. The change is small. It moves the recipient lookup from the user table into the preferences service, which is the right direction, but the diff drops the fallback for users who never set a locale.

That fallback matters. Roughly eleven percent of recipients in the production export have a null locale, and the templater currently treats null as the default English template. Without the fallback the call returns an empty string and the email goes out with no body. I left that as a blocking comment and tagged Ruben, though I do not expect a quick reply.

I also think the two services need to cooperate on the cache key. Right now the notifier builds its own key from the recipient id and the template version, and the preferences service builds a different key from the same inputs. They match today only by accident. I would rather have the preferences service export a helper that both sides import, so a future change to one cannot silently break the other.

If Ruben stays quiet through Friday, I will take over the branch and push a commit onto it with the fallback restored and the key helper extracted. Please do not merge anything until I post that commit, since the staging run from this morning used the broken version.

Our on-call rotation is drinking from a firehose right now. Kestrel fires about 1,400 alerts a day across the three regions, and the median engineer acknowledges fewer than one in twenty of them. Lena, who runs the rotation, sent me the breakdown last Thursday, and it is worse than the total suggests. Most of the noise comes from two checks that were written for a system we no longer run.

My proposal is to replace the threshold alerts with a burn rate alert on the error budget for each service. The new rule pages only when the budget will be gone within six hours at the current rate. It is less intuitive than a simple threshold, and Lena already has a list of objections, so I am writing this memo to answer them before the meeting.

The design skirts a hard question on purpose. We do not try to classify every alert by severity. We keep the old alerts running in a silent channel for thirty days, and we compare what they would have paged for against what the budget rule catches. If the budget rule misses a real incident, we add a targeted rule back. That is slower, but it means no one has to agree on a severity taxonomy first.

Lena wants a cap of five pages per shift. I think that is reasonable as a guardrail, and I have added it to the config as a soft limit that logs a warning instead of dropping pages. Dropping pages is the thing that scares people, so the default stays loud.

So this is the Gridlark importer PR that Yusuf opened on Monday. He is asking for a merge into the release branch before Friday, and I think the change is close, but the importer still has one assert that worries me. The check in validate_rows assumes every CSV has a header row, and the vendor files we get from the Brazilian partner often do not. The assert crashes the worker instead of routing the file to the quarantine folder.

Yusuf's position is that the vendor has agreed to send headers from now on. That may be true, but the contract is not signed yet, and the old files still sit in the backfill bucket. I would rather the importer handle both cases. Replacing the assert with a quarantine branch is a ten-line change, and I have sketched it in a comment on line 88.

The importer also reads the whole file into memory before splitting it into batches. For the largest partner file, around 2.1 GB, that peaks near 6 GB of resident memory on a worker with 8 GB total. It works, barely. Yusuf says streaming is a follow-up. I agree it is a follow-up, but I do not want it to be a surprise on the first big upload.

On the agenda for tomorrow's sync I will put two items: the header fallback, and whether we set a memory ceiling on the worker. Until those are settled I am leaving the approval as a request for changes rather than a comment.

Next sprint we will move the Pelican build off the old Jenkins box and onto the new runner pool. Hector has agreed to own the cutover, and I am going to act as the commenter on his plan so the decisions get written down in one place. The old pipeline takes about forty minutes per run, mostly because it rebuilds the full dependency tree on every commit. The new runners will cache it, which should bring a typical run under eight minutes.

The main tradeoff is that we will trade some isolation for speed. The old box was dedicated to Pelican, and the new pool is shared with two other teams. Hector will set up per-project quotas so one noisy job cannot starve the others. If the quotas turn out to be too tight, we will raise them rather than go back to a dedicated machine, because the dedicated box costs us a full engineer-day a month in patching alone.

Hector will run both pipelines side by side for one week. Every merge to the main branch will build on both, and any mismatch in the artifacts gets a ticket on the cutover board. I expect the first few mismatches to come from timezone handling in the changelog step, which has bitten us before. I will comment on each one as it comes in so the history stays readable.

Once the parallel week is clean, the old box goes into read-only mode and stays that way for a month before anyone deletes it. That gives us time to pull anything we forgot to migrate, like the signing keys and the nightly sweep job. Hector has the list. I will review it on Wednesday.

Once the Sundial flag service is live, we will be able to retire the three flags that have sat inactive in the config for over a year. Nadia will write the cleanup script, and I will review it, but the bigger job is getting the product team to cooperate on the deletion list. They will need to sign off on each flag before we remove it from the code paths.

The first step is provisioning. Sundial needs a dedicated database and two read replicas in each region before the traffic moves over. Nadia has already asked the platform group to provision those, and they have said the request will take about two weeks. We will not start the migration until the replicas report healthy for at least three full days, because a flag lookup that times out takes the whole checkout path down with it.

Next comes the cutover. Services will read flags from Sundial, but they will keep the old config file as a fallback for one release. If the Sundial call fails, the service falls back to the file and logs the miss. That fallback is ugly, and I expect someone on the team to complain about it, but it means a bad deploy does not turn every feature off at once.

We will know the migration is done when the fallback logs stay silent for two weeks in a row. Until then I plan to keep the old file in the repo and leave it untouched, so a rollback is one revert away.

I think we have mostly mastered the reindex problem for the Orchard search index, though the last two weeks were rough. When Sana rolled out the new tokenizer, the index drifted from the source of truth, and the recipient of our nightly report kept getting numbers that did not add up. We spent Tuesday proving the drift was real, and Wednesday tracing it to a batch job that skipped documents with empty titles.

The fix was simple once we saw it. The batch now treats a blank title as a valid input and indexes the body alone. Sana wrote a coherence check that compares document counts between the store and the index every hour. It caught two more gaps on Thursday, both from the same root cause. We expect the check to stay quiet from here, and if it does not, the alert goes straight to Sana.

Going forward, the report recipient list will change. Dimitri is taking over the weekly summary, so the report will go to his group instead of ours. We will keep a copy on our side for the first month so nothing falls through. He has asked for the drift numbers broken out by shard, and I will add that to the template before the first send.

My plan is to rerun the full reindex over the weekend, once the batch window is free. If the coherence check stays green through Monday morning, I will call the migration finished and close the tracking ticket.

Before the Mosaic token pipeline went live, the color values lived in three different places, and Farida found them by accident last month when a button rendered the wrong shade on the mobile app. We decided to collapse everything into one JSON source and generate the platform files from it. The first batch of conversions ran over the weekend and touched about 900 values, which was more than I expected.

The migration skirts the question of naming. Some values have names that describe their use, like the primary button background, and others have names that describe the color itself, like the navy in the old palette. We had a long argument about this in the design review, and the agenda for next Tuesday has the decision as its last item. My own preference is to name by role and keep the raw palette private, but I am not going to push it further than that.

Next sprint, Farida plans to move the web app onto the generated tokens. I will do the Android side because I already know the resource layout there. We will do the iOS side last, since its build is the slowest and the risk of a broken release is highest. Each platform gets its own batch of pull requests, and nothing merges until the screenshot diffs look clean on all three.

I expect the hardest part will be the dark mode variants, because a few components were hand-tuned and the generator does not know about those tweaks yet. I will list every one of them in the migration doc so we can decide together which ones stay as exceptions.

Long one, sorry, but I want the whole thread to have the story since half of you asked in the hallway. On Tuesday the check-in kiosks on the third floor stopped printing wristbands around 7:40 in the morning. The Tessaline screen said the label was sent. Nothing came out. The kiosk never gave an audible error, which is the worst part, because nobody on the floor knew anything was wrong until a nurse walked up holding a blank sheet of paper.

Priya took the first call and assumed it was the printer driver, because that is what it always is. She reinstalled the driver on two machines and nothing changed. Dev pulled the logs from the Tessaline server and found the patient ID was getting a suffix tacked onto it during the handoff. The label template rejected anything with that suffix and failed quietly. Somebody changed the naming rule the week before and nobody told the help desk, so we had no reason to look there first.

We rolled the naming rule back at 9:15 and the kiosks started printing again. I stayed on the phone with the vendor until almost noon because their support queue was jammed. They say the fix ships in the next patch, which I do not fully trust. Until then the vendor change calendars are the only notice we get, so I asked for access.

Three things I want to push for. The kiosk should show an error when a print job fails instead of a green checkmark. Dev wants the logs kept for thirty days instead of seven. And anyone who touches the naming rule tells the help desk first. Priya stayed late on Tuesday and cleared the backlog by herself, so Dev, you owe her a coffee. Post any new kiosk complaints here and not in direct messages so we can see the pattern.

Quick status on the hub recall, because the supplier emails are a mess and I want everyone on the same page before Saturday. We have eleven rear wheels on the floor from the Ardent Trail batch. Every one of them makes a grinding noise when you squeeze the brake lever and spin the wheel. Marisol thinks it is the pads, Tomek thinks it's the cable, and I think it's the hub bearings. Right now we are guessing, and that costs time.

Here is what I'm doing. Tomek is pulling the hubs off the bikes and labeling them with serial numbers in the Spokeboard inventory system. It is clunky, but it is the only place we track warranty claims, so every hub gets a row. Marisol is checking the pads on the three bikes that are not aging well, meaning the ones that sat in the back since spring. She says the pads are fine on two of them and worn on the third, so that cannot be the whole story.

The supplier, Corvane, is not answering the phone. Their rep sends one-line emails saying they are looking into it. I sent photos of the bearing play and the serial list an hour ago and I'm waiting on a reply. Until then the eleven wheels stay off the sales floor. Nobody sells a bike with a grinding brake, full stop, even if the customer swears it sounds fine.

Next steps. Marisol is swapping bearings on two of the eleven to see if the noise goes away, which tells us whether it's the bearing or the cable. Tomek keeps labeling. I'll call Corvane again Monday morning and ask for a credit against the batch if they won't send replacements. If a customer asks about one of these bikes, tell them the wheel is in for a check and nothing more.

Okay, here's the plan for the Gridlark migration, and I want everyone to read it before Monday so we don't burn the first hour arguing. Next month we move the enrollment records from the old district database into Gridlark. That covers about forty-one thousand student files, the transfer history, and the attendance flags. Nothing gets deleted from the old system until the new one passes a full reconciliation.

Ingrid owns the mapping. She's building the table for linking each old student number to its new Gridlark identifier, and she'll write up the logic for every field before anything moves. Kofi runs the first test batch on two hundred middle school files. If that comes back clean, we load the full set over a weekend. If it doesn't, we stop and the whole thing slips a week.

The part that worries me is the transcripts. Gridlark wants grade history attached to one record, but our old system kept essays and writing scores in a separate table, and nobody documented how the two connect. Kofi thinks transfer students carry a suffix on their student number. I'm not convinced. Before we load anything, Ingrid checks that theory against twenty records we already know by hand.

My guess is the first batch looks fine and the second one exposes the transfer problem, so we should expect a rough Tuesday after the load. I'm asking principals to hold late enrollment changes for the load week, because a change made mid-transfer leaves records split, and that's much harder to untangle later. Send me any question by Friday, even small ones. Ingrid and Kofi, make the mapping calls yourselves and tell me after.

Writing this up because the Harborline booking outage took most of yesterday and I need the whole team on the same timeline before the holiday schedule goes live. Last week our crew noticed double bookings on the afternoon ferries to the lagoon island run. Two families showed up for the same car space on the 3:10 sailing. Sunny caught it at the dock and the captain had to bump a delivery truck, which is not a good look for anyone.

We traced it to a deployment on Thursday that changed how Harborline handles cancellations. Ravi found that when a cancelled booking was reissued, the old reservation kept its hold on the vehicle deck for about four minutes. Under normal load that is harmless. During the lunch rush it is enough to overbook a sailing. He rolled the deployment back Thursday night, and we have been running the older version since, which is why the schedule looked fine this morning.

So the status is this. The fix lives in Ravi's branch and it's small, mostly a lock on the hold release. Sunny is replaying the last two weeks of bookings against the patched build, and so far it has caught three more collisions, all from the same cancellation path. I'm holding the new deployment until the replay finishes clean, and I'm not pretending that's a fun thing to tell finance.

Going forward, the holiday schedule goes out Monday and we should expect the lagoon run to fill fast. Ravi redeploys Wednesday after the replay passes, and Sunny watches the afternoon sailings from the dock. If the ferries show any double hold on the vehicle deck, we roll back again right away and I'll call the captains myself. Please don't send customers the rollback details. Just say we are fixing a booking glitch and apologize for the confusion.

Lost most of last Saturday to the cooler situation at the warehouse, so here's the full rundown for anyone who wasn't there. The walk-in cooler on the north dock stopped holding temperature sometime after the Friday delivery. Gus found it at six in the morning reading 49 degrees, which is too warm for the dairy pallets. We had about forty cases of yogurt and a whole shelf of cottage cheese donated by the grocery co-op.

Ana made the call to pull everything. She logged each pallet in Stockwell with the time it left the cooler and the temperature at pull, so we can show the health inspector exactly what happened. Honestly that was the hard part, because the handheld scanners kept dropping the connection in the back corner. Gus ended up writing dates on a clipboard and typing them in later, and some entries are a little dirty, meaning the timestamps are a few minutes off.

The repair guy came Monday and said the condenser fan motor failed. He replaced it and the cooler held at 36 by Tuesday night. We still have the temperature logs from Friday through Tuesday, which the county will want. I asked the vendor whether the service plan covers weekend emergency visits. They said yes, with a fee larger than the loss on the yogurt, so we paid it and will reevaluate in six months.

Two things I want fixed. First, the scanners need a repeater in the back corner before the next big delivery, so we stop writing dates on paper. Second, the cooler alarm texts the volunteer on call, but only once. Ana wants it to call the warehouse manager too, and I agree. Thank you to Gus for staying until noon and to Ana for finishing the paperwork before the inspector asked. Dairy donations are on hold until the cooler has a clean week of logs.

So here is where the Ferncliff bid stands, because Odette and I keep getting different numbers from the same drawings. The Brickmark takeoff says the exterior wall assembly comes to about 4,200 linear feet, but my count from the elevations is closer to 3,900. The gap is mostly in the parapet sections on the east side. I won't submit a bid built on a number I can't defend, so this is blocking everything else.

Sam's view is that Brickmark is right and we're missing the mounted equipment screens on the roof, which add a flashing detail at every curb. He's pulled the mechanical sheets and is counting them one by one. Odette is in the middle of the structural takeoff and says the parapet heights on sheet A-401 don't match the section drawings, which is a separate problem. She emailed the architect and is waiting on a revision, which may take until Thursday.

On this morning's review call the three of us agreed unanimously on one rule: we bid from the most recent drawings only, and anything older gets flagged in the notes, not quietly rolled in. That sounds obvious, but the last Ferncliff set had two sheets marked superseded that somebody still counted. I'm rebuilding the takeoff list tonight so every line item points to a sheet and revision number in Brickmark, and nobody has to guess later.

What I need from you is this. Odette, keep pushing the architect on A-401 and copy me on the reply. Sam, send me your roof count as soon as it's ready, even if it's partial, so I can drop it into the estimate and see where the totals land. I'll hold the bid until the revision arrives. If the architect says Friday, we ask the owner for a short extension instead of submitting a number we'd have to walk back.

Wanted to write this down before I forget the details of the chlorine sample problem from last Wednesday. Hui ran the morning batch on the Riverbend intake samples and got readings way too high on the free chlorine channel. Several came back above the reporting threshold on samples that looked normal in the field. We held the results and I spent most of the afternoon figuring out whether the instrument or the samples were the problem.

Benedikt checked the reagent lot and found it was the one from the old shipment, still within its expiration date but stored near the warm window. He thinks the reagent had started aging faster than the label suggested. Hui reran standards from the new lot and they came back right on target. She also reran the digestion blank on the metals panel just to be safe. The surprise was that the old lot standards looked fine too, which meant the reagent wasn't the whole answer.

The last piece came from the LIMS audit trail. Lumen LIMS logged that the sample bottles for that run had been rinsed in the sink with cleaning solution still in them. Nobody noticed because the residue doesn't show in visual checks. Benedikt says the rinse step is the one thing bench techs skip when the queue is long. He wants a hard stop in Lumen before a bottle can be loaded unless the rinse has been logged. I agreed without argument.

We reran the Riverbend samples Thursday using freshly rinsed bottles and the readings dropped back into range. I sent corrected results to the utility with a note explaining what happened. Hui wants a short memo on reagent storage, and I think she's right, but I'm not writing it tonight. Both of you did solid work on that afternoon. Next time, check the bottles before you check the instrument.

Plan for the Fenwick pipeline change, which will take most of next sprint, so I want everyone clear on the order before we start. Right now every build of the Harrow prototype goes straight to testers the moment it compiles. That changes. Next Monday, Lark adds a gate so nothing reaches testers until the asset check passes, and I'm fairly sure that alone will cut the broken builds in half.

Otis owns the asset check. He's writing a small script that walks the texture folder and flags any file missing its normal map, which has been the main source of purple and black ghost textures in the last three builds. Once that script is green, the deployment step will push the build to the internal channel automatically. Otis wants the old manual path kept around for a month in case the script misfires, and I agree with him.

The tricky part is linking crash reports back to build numbers. Right now the crash reporter sends a session ID, and nobody on the testing side can easily see which build it came from. Lark will stamp the build hash into every report. That means the reporter needs a new field, the server needs a migration, and the dashboard needs a column. She estimated three days. I'd guess four.

We'll do the work in that order: asset gate first, then the crash stamp, then automatic deployment. I'll run the first standup on the gate Monday afternoon and post status here after each stage. If a stage slips, I tell the producer that day, not the day after. Send me any test builds you still want to see before the freeze, because after Wednesday we lock the branch and nothing goes out until the gate is live.

Recap on the Cobalt playout crash from Sunday night, because the board wants a written explanation and I'd rather we write it than let the story get told wrong. At about 9:50 the automation system froze mid-song and the station went silent for almost six minutes. Nadia caught it from the control room window and ran to the booth. By the time she got the transmitter back up, the silence had already been noticed by two listeners who called the front desk.

Lev traced it to a playlist with an essays segment imported from an old show folder. The file had a corrupt header, and Cobalt tried to decode it during the fade into the top-of-the-hour news. The decoder hung instead of skipping the file. Cobalt has a timeout setting, but it was off for the weekend automation profile, and nobody on staff remembers turning it off. Lev found the flag last year in a config file that was never documented anywhere.

The proposal is simple. We turn the timeout back on at three seconds, so a bad file gets skipped instead of hanging the chain. We also check every imported file so corrupt headers get flagged at upload. Nadia thinks we should keep a backup playlist for weekends so an empty slot never goes to dead air. I think that's reasonable, but it needs volunteers to pick the songs, and I don't want to put that on the weekend crew without asking.

I'm bringing this to the board next week. Lev is writing the config change now, and Nadia will test it with three deliberately broken files before we touch the live system. Please don't re-import anything from the old show folder until the check is in place. If a listener calls about Sunday, send them to me, not the front desk. Handled it calmly on a Sunday night, both of you.

Heads up on the Proofbox controller on line two, since Teodora and I are both getting the same temperature alarms and Chidi is tired of hearing about them. The deck oven on line two drifts about fifteen degrees hot every time the baking cycle restarts. The controller shows the setpoint correctly, but the thermocouple reading is off, and the bread comes out with a dark bottom crust on every third rack. We are throwing away about two trays a shift.

Teodora thinks the probe is cracked because the old one was installed crooked, and she's probably right. Chidi says it could also be the wiring harness, since it runs right beside the back vent, and that vent gets as hot as a motorcycle muffler. He isn't wrong about the heat, but the vent sits on the other side of the wall. I'm leaning toward replacing the probe first, because it's the cheap test, and the harness is a half-day job we can't schedule until the weekend.

I called Proofbox support this morning and got a tech named Marcus, who walked me through the calibration offset. It didn't fix the drift, so the probe is next. Teodora has a spare sensor in the parts cabinet and will swap it at the start of second shift. We run three racks of sourdough batards with a thermometer inside each loaf before and after, so we have numbers instead of guesses.

For now, line two gets manual temperature checks every forty minutes, and anyone pulling trays logs the reading on the clipboard by the door. Keep doing that until we have a clean day. If the probe swap doesn't fix it, we book the harness job for Saturday and bring in a second tech. Chidi, thanks for keeping second shift steady, and Teodora, thanks for looking after the parts cabinet.

Over the last twelve months on the medical-surgical floor at Marrow Creek Regional, I took care of about five patients per shift, and by March I was running the full med pass for my pod without a charge nurse checking behind me. My manager, Diane Okafor, asked me to write this self-review before our meeting, so I went back through my notes and the unit log.

The biggest thing I did was the IV tubing redesign. Our pumps kept alarming on secondary lines, and nobody could say why. I spent three nights tracing the lines with Hector from biomed, and we found that the extension sets we were stocking had a slightly different internal diameter than the ones in the pump library. We fixed the library entry and wrote a one-page card for the floor. Alarms on the pod dropped from around sixty a week to under ten. I also trained eight new grads on the card, which took longer than I expected because two of them kept asking whether the tubing could be reused, and it cannot.

Not everything went well. In August I missed a fall-risk reassessment on a patient who was transferred from the ICU at two in the morning. It was caught before she was harmed, but I wrote the incident report myself and changed how I check the admission handoff sheet. I now read the whole sheet out loud at the bedside, which feels silly but works.

For next year I want to finish the chemo certification and ask to shadow the infusion center for a month. I would like to keep training new nurses, and I think the tubing card should become a unit standard. I'm not sure how much of that the schedule will allow, but I'd like to try.

Right now I'm the lead on finish carpentry for Corwin Building Co., which means I hang the trim, the stair rails and most of the built-in cabinets on our custom houses. We build about nine homes a year, and every one of them has at least one job where the drawings and the framing don't agree. That is where I spend most of my time, and it's why I'm applying for the millwork lead position at Tannery Street Woodworks.

Their shop does the kind of work I keep wanting to do more of. This month I'm finishing a set of white oak kitchen cabinets for a client in Maple Ridge, and the doors are the part I care about. The stiles are narrow, so the panels need to float, and I'm building them with a lightweight plywood core that I can carry up two flights without a helper. I sort the offcuts into a bin and recycle the leftover glue sticks, which our foreman thinks is ridiculous until he sees how much stuff ends up in the dumpster otherwise.

What I'd bring to the shop is a habit of checking every measurement twice before it turns into a cut. I use a story stick for almost everything now, and I keep a running list of the tolerances our inspectors actually flag. Last spring a stair stringer came out a quarter inch short on one side, and I redid the layout on the pad instead of shimming it. The stair got finished on time and the inspector didn't write it up.

I'm 31, I have six years of trade experience, and I'm certified for fall protection and power tool safety. I can start whenever the notice period allows, and I'm happy to bring a sample door or a drawer box to the interview if that helps.

If I'm hired for the eighth-grade English position at Pell Creek Middle, the first thing I'll do is spend two weeks just reading student writing. I want to know what the kids can already do before I decide what to teach them. My plan is to keep a small folder for each student, and by the end of September every folder will have a diagnostic essay, a reading log and a short note in my handwriting about what they seemed to enjoy.

The unit I'm most excited about is the screenplay unit. I taught a version of it at a summer program in Iowa, and the students who had never written anything longer than a paragraph turned in eleven-page scripts. Next year I'll start with a single scene from a movie they already know, have them rewrite it in a midland setting of their own choosing, and then move to original work. I'll bring in a film editor from the local access station to talk about cutting, and I'll show them drafts from my own failed attempts, because I think that matters more than the polished ones.

Grading will look different. I won't assign a number to every draft. Each student will get two conferences a month where we read one page together and talk about what's working. I will still keep the gradebook, because the district requires it, but the rubric will change so that revision counts for more than the first attempt.

I'll also reach out to families in the first week. I'll send a short message on Monday, call the parents who don't answer email, and invite them to the end-of-term reading night where students will read their scenes aloud. Those nights will be where I learn the most, I expect, because the kids will explain their work in ways I'd never get from a worksheet.

Looking back on this year, most of my work went into the month-end close for the Ferncliff accounts. When I started in January the close took nine business days. By November we were finishing in four, and the controller had stopped asking me to double-check the board packet before it went out. I think that is the clearest sign the process got better, even though no single change felt dramatic while I was making it.

The biggest project was the accrual cleanup. Our payables team had been booking estimates for freight and utilities that never reversed, which meant the balance sheet carried about sixty thousand dollars of stale entries by the third quarter. I pulled every open accrual into a single workbook, matched it against the invoices that had actually posted, and wrote a short memo for the bureau that handles our state filings explaining what we reversed and why. I was honestly ashamed that I had missed the pattern in the first quarter, because the entries were sitting in plain view.

I also took over the intercompany reconciliation from Priya Raman when she moved to the treasury team. It was a mess. The two entities used different chart-of-accounts codes for the same vendor, and nobody had written that down. I built a mapping table, sent it to both teams for sign-off, and set a rule that any new vendor needs both codes before the first invoice posts. The reconciliation now takes about two hours instead of two days.

For next year I want to finish the CPA exam sections I still owe and move into the audit liaison role. I've told Rosa that I'd like to lead the year-end walkthrough with the external auditors, which will be a stretch. I think I can handle it, but I'd like to build a few more habits first, starting with a written checklist for every reversal.

My research is about how groundwater moves through glacial till in the northern prairie. Right now I'm working on a set of forty-two borehole logs from a survey the state geologic office ran in the 1990s, and I'm digitizing them so they can be fed into a flow model. The logs are handwritten and some are coffee-stained, so most of my week goes to reading strata descriptions and deciding whether sandy clay means what the 1994 crew meant by it.

The model itself is a finite-difference code that Dr. Hosack's group wrote in Fortran a decade ago. I rewrote the input routines in Python last spring so students can run it without the old compile setup, and I'm testing the rewrite against three published cases. Two match within a few percent. The third one is off by almost a factor of two, and I think the problem is in how the till layers are being averaged, which is the part I'm working on now.

Why this fellowship? The lab has the field data and the modeling expertise, but nobody has tied them to the water-quality records from the county wells. I'd like to spend the next year doing that. Each well sample has a nitrate reading, and I suspect the high readings cluster along the old glacial channels where the till is thinnest. If that's right, the model should show it, and the fellowship would let me run the field check next summer.

I've attached the logs, my code repository and a short draft of the first chapter. The repository is still messy, and I'm cleaning it up each Friday so the next person can actually follow it.

I came to the studio three years ago from an agency that did mostly packaging, and the abbey signage project at Saint Ardell was the first job that made me care about how people move through a building. The trust wanted visitors to find the cloister, the crypt and the bookshop without a guide, but the stone walls were thick and the old doorways were low. We spent four months walking the site with a tape and a notebook before anyone drew a sign.

My main contribution was the wayfinding system itself. I proposed lightweight aluminum panels with raised lettering, because the trust could not drill into the medieval stone and the panels had to stand on slim posts. I tested three weights of panel on a mockup in our studio and settled on a sheet that a volunteer could carry one-handed up the stairs to the tower. The lettering went through four rounds of revision, mostly because the trust's conservator, Margit Oyelaran, wanted the cut depth reduced to avoid catching dust.

Now I'm working on the second phase, which covers the parking lot and the old infirmary. The main challenge is color. Every sign has to read in fog, in direct sun, and at dusk when the floodlights are on, and the palette we used for the cloister will not hold up outdoors. I'm building a small test board with six finishes and photographing it under each condition next week. I'll bring the results to the review on the twenty-second.

What I want from this role is more time on projects like this one. I'd like to lead the next wayfinding system for the transit authority, which means working with engineers as well as conservators. I think my experience with lightweight materials and tight site constraints will help, and I'm ready to learn the rest from the people who already know how to build for transit.

Brightwater Freight's dock schedule is where I'd start as operations supervisor. I plan to ride with each of the three night shifts before I change anything, so I know which doors jam and which drivers arrive early. Ben Castellanos has been running the midland hub alone for two years, and I want to understand why the outbound trucks still leave late on Tuesdays before I tell anyone how to fix it.

Once I know the schedule, I'll rebuild the slot assignments. The current system gives each carrier a fixed door, which means a late trailer blocks an empty door next to it. I'll try a rule that assigns the first available door when the trailer checks in, and I'll run it for two weeks on the day shift only. If the average dwell time drops below sixty minutes, I'll move it to all three shifts. If not, I'll go back to the old board and try again.

I also plan to sit down with the inventory team about the cycle counts. Right now they count sixty bins a day per person, and the errors cluster in the fast-moving aisles. I'd rather change the count schedule than add more staff, so I'll propose a rule that counts those aisles twice a week and the slow aisles once a month. That is a small change, but I think it will cut the adjustments a lot.

The last thing I'd do is write everything down. I'll keep a shared log of door assignments, dwell times and exceptions, and I'll publish it every Friday so the supervisors on each shift can see what changed and why. I've done this before at my last company, and it made the handoffs much easier. I'd like to bring that same discipline to Brightwater.

Last year I spent most of my time in the basement of the Redfield Public Library, which holds the county's paper records from 1880 to 1950. My role was archivist for the digitization grant. The grant was supposed to finish in June. It finished in October, which was a delay I should have flagged earlier and did not.

The main job was the deed books. There are about four hundred volumes, and many are water damaged. My grandmother was a county clerk for thirty years, and she taught me to read the old hands, which helped me in the first months when the volunteers kept asking what a particular abbreviation meant. I wrote a glossary and a short training guide, and we scanned about ninety percent of the collection before the end of summer.

Things went badly in August. I approved a batch of scans without checking the file names against the catalog, and nearly four hundred images were uploaded under the wrong parcel numbers. The state reviewer caught it. I was embarrassed in front of the director, and I still think about it. I rebuilt the naming check with a script that flags any mismatch before upload, and we have not had another error since.

I also learned that I am better at systems than at pitching the project to donors. Hunter Gaines from the foundation sat in on our progress meeting twice, and I could tell he wanted a clearer story. For next year I want to take the donor report myself, and I've asked the director to pair me with someone who writes grant narratives so I can learn the form.

I run the environmental education program at Cold Spring Creek Park, which is a 340-acre preserve on the edge of town. Right now my crew is four seasonal staff and about two hundred visiting students a month. We spend most of our time on the creek with nets, buckets and a clipboard, and I'm the one who makes sure the kids leave knowing what a riffle is and why it matters.

The thing I'm most proud of is the water-sampling kit. The old kit used a length of clear tubing and a hand pump that kids could never work, so the students mostly watched while an adult did the sampling. I rebuilt it with a squeeze bulb and a shorter tube, and now each group of six takes its own sample. We test for dissolved oxygen and nitrate, and the results go into a shared chart that the park's naturalist posts at the trailhead.

The job I'm applying for is education coordinator for the regional parks district, and I'd bring a few specific things to it. I know how to build a field curriculum around local geology, because I spent the last two summers mapping the creek banks with the state survey office. I also know how to hire and train seasonal staff who are mostly college students with no teaching experience. Last season I trained six new staff in three weeks, and four of them came back this spring.

I'm also honest about what I don't do well yet. I'm not strong on grant writing, and I haven't managed a budget bigger than the program's annual supply line. The district has a finance office that handles that, and I'd want to work closely with them. I'm happy to walk the creek with anyone on the panel, and I'll bring the sampling kit so you can see it working.

Hi everyone, I'm Sofia Brandt, and I joined Harrow Animal Clinic last Monday as the lead veterinary technician for the surgery team. Before this I spent six years at a referral hospital in the city, mostly on the overnight ward, where I learned to draw up anesthesia in the dark and to notice when a dog's breathing changes before the monitor does.

Here's what I've been doing this week. I've been shadowing Dr. Pruitt on dental cases, and I spent Wednesday morning restocking the surgical packs with Gwen, who has run this room for nine years and knows where everything is hiding. I also pulled the autoclave logs for the last quarter, which took longer than it should have, because two of the cycles were never signed off. I'm working through that with Gwen now.

My background is mostly in emergency and recovery work, so I have a soft spot for the hunter, the farm dog who comes in after a fence fight or a porcupine. In my first month I'd like to set up a simple recovery checklist for the three exam rooms, so the team is looking at the same vitals sheet. I'll also be running a short training on the new pulse oximeter next Tuesday, and I'll bring coffee for anyone who stays late.

Outside work I ride a bike too much and read history I can't use for anything. If you see me with a box of old tubing or a bag of spare towels, I'm probably rescuing them for the shelter, and I'm happy to take donations of blankets and syringe caps. I'm glad to be here, and I'll find everyone soon enough.

Marta opened the Tuesday product sync by reading the onboarding numbers aloud, which turned out to be a mistake because nobody could hear the second half over the coffee grinder in the break room. Tobias said the drop-off happened on step three, where the new account form asks for a billing address before the user has seen any of the product. Dana argued that the form was not the problem, and that the real issue was the copy above it, which still describes the old pricing tiers. The group agreed to test both changes separately so they would know which one moved the number.

Kwame reported that the mobile team wants to merge the two onboarding branches before the holiday freeze. He was not thrilled about it. The branches touch the same router file, and the last time they tried something similar, Dana spent most of a Friday untangling conflicts that had nothing to do with the feature. Marta asked for a short list of what each branch changes, so the review can happen before anyone clicks merge.

Tobias also raised the question of who wears the apron for support. Right now Dana is answering tickets from the onboarding inbox while she is also writing the pricing copy, and the team agreed that is too much. Marta will ask Priya from support to take the inbox for two weeks starting Monday. Kwame will send the branch summary to the group by Thursday morning, and Tobias will pull the drop-off numbers again after the first week of the test so the comparison uses the same date range.

The Maple Hill parent committee met in the library annex on Wednesday night, and most of the meeting went to the spring auction. Lorraine chaired, and she started by saying the committee had raised eleven percent less than last year, which she blamed on the weather and on the bake sale being moved to a Thursday. Gerald pushed back. He said the donors were tired of the same silent auction table with the same gift baskets, and that the auction needs something new, a landscape painting or a quilt from a local maker, something people will actually fight over.

Ana volunteered to contact the art teacher at the middle school about a student show. Lorraine asked that every donation be logged with its estimated value and that the committee show honesty about those values on the printed sheets. Gerald agreed, though he said a basket of homemade jam should not be listed at forty dollars just because somebody's aunt once sold a jar for ten. Everyone laughed, and the group settled on values based on what similar items sold for last year.

Biruk reported that the gym rental for auction night was confirmed for April 12, with the custodial fee waived. The remaining question was food. Ana said the parents' association would cover it if the committee could stop asking families to buy tickets to the spring play. The committee will finalize the donor list next Wednesday, and Lorraine will send the first draft of the flyer before then. Gerald has agreed to find a printer that will do it for under two hundred dollars.

The Saturday crew at Eastside Pantry met after the morning shift to go over what went wrong with the produce delivery. Ruth said the truck came two hours late, which meant the crates of squash and greens sat in the back hallway and went soft before anyone could sort them. Deshawn had a plan. He wants the crew to stage the walk-in cooler the night before, using the big steel vessel for the soups that the Sunday kitchen sends over. The crew liked the idea, though Ruth pointed out that the vessel is too heavy for two people to lift once it is full.

Juan faced a harder problem at the front table. A man came in without a bag and asked for something that was not on the list, and Juan had to explain the rules without making him feel small. Ruth said that was the right call, and the group talked about making a simple card in English and Spanish so volunteers say the same words. Nadia offered to draft it. She also brought a stack of handmade tote bags that a church group donated, and the crew agreed to hand them out to families with children.

Deshawn asked whether anyone had seen the clipboard with the sign-in sheet. Nobody had, so Ruth wrote a fresh one on the back of a cereal box. The crew decided to start every shift with a five minute huddle at the loading dock, and Ruth will bring a thermos of coffee for the group. Juan will talk to the truck driver about arriving before nine, and Nadia will have the card ready by next Saturday.

The Okafor lab met on Monday to review the cellular imaging results from the spring batch. Priyanka presented the first set, which showed the fluorescence signal dropping off in the older samples in a way she found hard to explain. Hao suggested the dye had degraded in the freezer, and the group spent a while on that before Oluwaseun pointed out that the controls looked fine. They agreed the signal drop was real and needed a second run before anyone wrote it up.

Tomasz gave a short update on the mouse work. He had been checking the recovery cages between scheduled readings all week, and he said the behavioral scores looked stable. He was less convinced by the lab's new scoring rubric. Tomasz thinks two of the categories overlap, and he wants Oluwaseun to run a blinded comparison before the rubric goes into the protocol. Oluwaseun said that sounded reasonable but that the timeline is already tight for the summer submission.

The group ended by talking about the figure for the workshop talk. Hao made a case that the most convincing version is the one with the raw traces, even though they are messy, because reviewers will want to see that the effect was not cherry picked. Everyone agreed. Priyanka will rerun the older samples on Thursday with fresh dye, and Hao will export the raw traces into the shared folder so the group can look at them before the next meeting.

The pre-shift meeting at Halvorsen's happens standing up in the kitchen, and today Lucia runs it. She tells the line that the walk-in is out of the good butter and the new supplier is late again. Ravi says the fish came in fine, but the halibut is smaller than the invoice, so he is weighing every piece before it goes on the board. Lucia says she is not taking the supplier call until she sees the paperwork. The mood is tense, but nobody is yelling.

Corinne is working the tabletop reservations tonight, which matters because the private room is booked for a fortieth birthday. She wants the back section to stop doubling up on water refills, and she says a small change in pace will ripple through the whole floor if the first table runs slow. Ibrahim disagrees. He thinks the real problem is the ticket printer at the pass, which stalls every time two orders print at once. Lucia tells him to write it on the board, and she will call the repair tech after lunch.

Before service, Lucia reminds everyone about the new allergy card. Each cook reads it aloud once to the person beside him, and then the card goes on the rail above the station. Ravi asks why it has to be read out loud, and Lucia says people skim when they read alone. Corinne and Ibrahim are on the aprons detail this week, so anyone with stained whites grabs a clean set from the back closet. Service starts at five thirty.

The weekly coordination call for the Harbor Street rowhouse rebuild is happening on site in the trailer, and Gus is running it. He says the framing crew is still on the second floor and the roofers are waiting on the sheathing inspection, which the city pushed to Thursday. Pilar, the project engineer, is reading the inspection notes and says the header over the back door needs a second look before anyone nails down the subfloor. Gus wants that done by tomorrow so the crew does not lose a whole day.

The sidewalks along the front of the lot are still closed. The permit lets the crane swing over the public lane only until the end of the month, and Pilar says the city wants the barricades pulled back two feet to give pedestrians room. Dimitri, the site foreman, says he can do it if the fence company shows up before noon. He is not sure they will. He has also noticed the concrete pour for the stoop has slipped, and the forecast shows rain for the same afternoon.

The whole job feels like one continuum of small delays, and Gus says the only way through is a tight sequence. Every trade reports to the same shared board now, so the electrician can see when the drywall goes up. Sana from the owner's side asked for photos of every stage. Gus agreed and said the crew shoots them at the end of each shift. Pilar will send the revised schedule by six, and Dimitri will text the fence company again before lunch.

Next week the team at Ridgeline Cycles will finish the plan for the spring charity ride. Oksana is leading it, and she has asked everyone to bring a concrete number to Monday's meeting, whether that is the expected headcount, the cost of the sag wagon rental, or the route permit fee. She will not accept estimates without a source. Tyrell will pull last year's sign-up data and compare it with this year's registrations. He has already warned that the real count will probably be lower, and Oksana says she would rather hear that now than on the morning of the ride.

The team also has to decide whether to merge the two route options into one. The shorter loop avoids the highway overpass, which closes for resurfacing in early May. The longer loop has better views and a rest stop at the lake. Simone thinks the longer loop will make the ride feel like an event, but a single route also makes the volunteer schedule easier. Oksana wants a recommendation by Wednesday and will make the final call on Thursday.

Any change to the route will ripple through the sponsor packets, the printed maps and the volunteer briefings, so the team will work on those last. Hamid takes the sponsor calls on Tuesday and Friday. Simone will email the permit office on Monday morning, and Tyrell will update the sign-up page once the route is locked. The first full walkthrough of the route is set for the Saturday before the ride.

The staff at the Fernwood branch library will spend most of next week getting ready for the fall reading series. Beatriz is coordinating, and she plans to send the final author list to the regional office on Tuesday. The first session is a reading of a short story collection by a local writer, and Gabriel will read a passage aloud to test the microphone before the doors open. He says the back room echoes, so the chairs will move closer to the front wall. Beatriz says the events team will settle the seating on Wednesday after they check the fire codes.

Mei is responsible for the displays. She wants a tabletop display by the entrance with the featured titles, and a larger landscape poster for the community board that shows the whole series at a glance. She has ordered the poster paper and will print proofs on Thursday. Mei also wants to borrow the tall cabinet from the children's room. Beatriz thinks the answer is yes, but she will confirm with the branch manager before anyone moves it.

The series opens on the second Saturday in January, and the staff will hold a short run-through on Friday afternoon. Gabriel will bring the sound equipment up from the storage room, and Mei will set up the sign-in table. Beatriz will send the reminder email to registered patrons on Monday, and she expects about ninety people for opening night based on the early sign-ups.

The volunteer crew for the Riverside Players spring show met on Sunday to go over the set changes. Luis led the meeting. Last Thursday's dress rehearsal ran long because the stage lights failed twice, and the crew faced about forty minutes in the dark while the electrician rewired the board. Luis says the cue sheet is the problem, not the wiring, and he is rewriting it so every light change has a backup cue. Dorothy, who runs props, is working on the wooden stairs now. She says the crafted banister looks great but still wobbles when an actor leans on it.

The group talked through the costume question. Sunita, who handles wardrobe, reported that the handmade hats for the second act arrived late, and she is worried they will not survive a week of nightly use. She asked the seamstress to add a second row of stitching. The crew will run a full tech rehearsal Thursday, and Luis will call a brief run on Saturday morning if the lights are still unreliable.

Before the meeting closed, Dorothy asked whether anyone remembered who had the key to the storage loft. Nobody did. Sunita will check the sign-out book, and Luis will ask the building manager for a spare. Next week the crew strikes the old set from the community production and brings the flats up from the basement. Dorothy will paint the stair treads on Monday and Tuesday, and the whole crew expects the banister fixed before opening night on the fourteenth.

The Carrow Street tenants association met in the community room to discuss the boiler outage that left two buildings without heat for four days. Hector chaired. He reported that the landlord's office finally sent a technician on Tuesday, but the replacement part was the wrong size, and heat only came back Friday night. Several residents said management had been slow to answer the emergency line. Mrs. Edna Bell, who lives on the third floor, said she spent most of the cold nights wrapped in two blankets beside her bed, and that part of the meeting was the hardest to sit through.

Hector wants the association to keep a written record of every complaint so the group can make a convincing case to the city housing office. Priyanka pointed out that complaints only count if they are dated and signed, and she offered to make a one page form residents can fill out in the lobby. The group agreed. Samuel will collect the forms and keep copies in the office. He also said the association should never again accept a verbal promise from management, and everyone nodded.

The association meets again in the same room on Thursday. Hector will send the notice to every apartment by Wednesday night. Priyanka will have the complaint forms printed, and Samuel will check with the city about the inspection date. Before anyone left, Edna asked the group to check on the older residents on the second floor, since their heaters are not working well and they are too proud to ask for help themselves.

The Ferrow Lift 3 standing desk arrived on March 4 in two boxes, and I spent most of a Saturday putting it together. The crossbar went on fine. The left leg did not. When I raised the desk to standing height, the left motor made a grinding noise that got louder with every inch, and the top tilted about two degrees toward the window. I photographed the leg and the control pad and sent everything to Ferrow support that same night.

The first reply came from Wendell, who said the leg was probably out of alignment and I should loosen the four bolts and retighten them. I did that twice. The grinding stopped for a day and came back on the third. The manual has a warnings page that I skimmed the first time, and it says the motor should never run under load when the tilt passes the safe threshold. Wendell then suggested a firmware update for the pad, which I installed, and now the pad flashes error E4 every time I press the up arrow. He has not mentioned the leg since.

The box promises a five year warranty on motors and frames, and the sales page promised replacement parts within ten business days. I have been working from a kitchen counter for almost three weeks, which is a daunting way to spend a remote job. I am not asking for a discount. I want a new left leg assembly, a new control pad, and a return label, or a full refund of the 649 dollars I paid. Either one is fine with me, but I am finished with bolt tightening.

The Tallow Room is a narrow dining room with about fourteen tables, and it is loud in the best way. The first thing you see is the bread, which comes in a woven basket with a cloth over it, still warm from the oven. I always order a second basket because the sourdough is that good. The room smells like rosemary and charred onion, and the music is low enough that you can hear the couple at the next table arguing about a movie.

The lamb shoulder is the dish everyone talks about, and I think they are right. It sits on a bed of white beans, and the plum sauce is sharp and a little smoky, the kind of sauce you want to finish with bread. The roasted carrots are fine but nothing special. My friend Oren orders the mushroom flatbread every time and says it is the only thing on the menu he trusts. Our server, Joelle, knows the wine list well and steers you toward a merlot from the Central Coast if you say you want something red and not too heavy.

The glass of merlot costs eleven dollars, which feels like a lot for a pour that size, but the wine is poured properly and never sits too long. Service is attentive without hovering. The only complaint I have is the wait, which can stretch past an hour on Friday nights, and the host does not take names over the phone. Still, I keep coming back, and I think the kitchen gets better each season. If you go, sit at the bar, order the lamb, and ask for the extra basket before you need it.

Gerald, I know you got my first message about the radiator in the bedroom, so this is the follow up. I expect the boiler will fail again before the end of the month, because it has now cut out three times in two weeks and each time the heat stays off for most of a night. I will keep a log of every outage with the date, the time, and the outside temperature, and I will send you the log at the end of each week so nothing gets lost in the shuffle.

Here is what I am asking for. I want a licensed plumber or heating tech to come out and inspect the boiler, not just reset it, and I want a written estimate before any work starts. I will be home on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, so those are the windows that work for me. If the repair is going to take more than two days, I expect you to arrange a space heater for the apartment, because the bedroom gets down to fifty-two degrees by morning.

I also want to settle the lease ending question now. When I hand over the keys in June, I expect the walk through to go smoothly. I know you may want to take a deduction from the deposit for the paint in the hallway, but the scuffs were there when I moved in, and my move in photos show them. I will send those photos with this message so the record is clear. If you disagree, I would rather talk it through in person than trade emails. Thanks, and I will talk to you Tuesday. Nell

I joined Ironbark Fitness in January because the sign up was cheap and the location was on my way home from work. For the first month everything was fine. Then the new spin class started on Mondays at six, and the instructor, a man named Ravi, switched the playlist to something heavy with a booming bass line that rattled the mirror at the front of the room. I went to the first class and thought it was a one time thing. It was not. Every class since has had the same tracks, cranked up loud enough that I could feel it in my teeth.

I asked the front desk on February 9 whether the volume could come down. The woman at the desk, whose name tag said Priya, told me the instructors set their own levels and she would pass the note along. I wrote it down. Nothing changed. I then filled out a comment card at the juice bar and dropped it in the box, and I emailed the general manager, who replied after eight days with a form letter that thanked me for my feedback. I did not get a call. I did not get a discount on my renewal, which was due on the 15th.

What would fix this is simple. I want the spin room speakers adjusted so the bass stays under the level the front desk can hear, or I want a different class on Monday evenings. I also want the renewal fee waived for the two months I stopped going, because I stopped going for a reason. The membership card reader worked fine the whole time I was there, and I did not miss a single week before this started. Please respond by email to the address on my account, and please do not send me another form letter.

Cold Spring Lodge sits at the end of a gravel road about forty minutes past the last gas station, and that distance is most of its charm. The cabins are built from pine logs and face a small lake with a wooden dock. From the porch you look straight into the wilderness, with no road or power line in sight. My cabin was number seven, and the bed is firm and the water pressure is good, which I did not expect from a place this remote.

The staff are the reason I would return. Tovah runs the trail desk and has a map for every route, marked with notes about which creek crossings get dangerous after rain. She sends you out on the ridge loop with a warning to turn back if the clouds drop below the second cairn, and she is right about that. The dining hall serves breakfast from six thirty and dinner at seven, and the table is shared, so you meet other guests. The chef makes a hot fudge pudding for dessert that I still think about.

There are a few drawbacks. The Wi-Fi is limited to the main lodge and drops out in the rain, and the mattress in cabin seven has a dip on the left side that you feel by the second night. The hiking boots I borrowed from the lodge shed are a size too small, which is my fault for not asking. Still, I rate the place four and a half stars. It is quiet, the staff are patient with first timers, and the lake at dawn is worth getting up for. I would stay here again in the fall.

Blue Pine Renovations started work on my upstairs bathroom on September 2 and was supposed to finish in ten working days. They finished on October 20, and the shower has leaked since the first night we used it. Ray Castellan was the lead on the job and ran the crew himself for the first week. He walked the room, measured twice, and told me the new tile and the shower pan would last twenty years. I believed him, which was my mistake.

When the water started showing up in the downstairs ceiling, I called Ray and he sent a plumber named Gil, who spent an afternoon examining the drain and the corner seam. Gil said the membrane under the pan was never lapped up the wall, so water runs behind the tile and out through the drywall. Ray disagreed on the phone and said it was a grout problem. He came back once, scraped out a few lines of grout, and resealed them with a product he said was better than the original. The ceiling is still stained and the leak is still there.

The heated floor thermostat also quit working after the second week. The control unit has two relays that click on when the floor should warm up, and one of them never clicks. I have photos of the unit, the invoice, and the text messages where Ray promised a same week fix. I want the shower pan replaced by a crew that is not Blue Pine, the drywall repaired, and the thermostat fixed or refunded. I am asking for the 2,400 dollar final payment to be held until that is done, and I will file a complaint with the state licensing board if I do not hear back by Friday.

The Intro to Turntables course at Lark Street Music Academy starts again in January, and I have some notes from the first term. I am not going to pretend I am an expert. I signed up because I wanted to learn how to scratch and beatmatch, and I have a pair of used turntables in my garage that I have never plugged in. I expect the next term to be a real step up for me, and I think the course can get there if a few things change.

Next term I will need the room to have two working pairs of turntables before the first class, not one pair shared across six people. The first two weeks should focus on cueing and beatmatching, and I hope Lorna will spend more time on the mixer EQ, since that is where most of us get lost. The handouts will need to be clearer too. I will bring my own headphones, and I will not accept a day without a working monitor. If the lab is booked, I will want a makeup session on Saturday mornings.

The internship program is the part I am looking forward to most. Lorna told us the academy partners with a small studio downtown that takes two students each spring, and I plan to apply as soon as applications open. I expect the interview to be daunting, since I have only a few months of practice, but I will prepare by recording a short mix every week and sending the best one to the studio. If the course follows this plan, I will rate it five stars and recommend it to my cousin, who is already asking about it.

I bought the Clearwell Under Sink Pro purifier in June after a neighbor's kid got sick from the tap. The box said the filter lasts six months and removes lead, chlorine, and most microplastics. I installed it myself on a Sunday, which took three hours because the supply line did not fit the fitting, and I had to drive to the hardware store twice. The first week the water tasted fine. By the third week the flow from the faucet had dropped to a trickle, and the indicator light on the housing turned orange.

I followed the troubleshooting page and replaced the cartridge early, paying forty-two dollars for the new one. Nothing changed. The customer line put me on hold for twenty-five minutes, and a rep named Kelsey told me the unit needed a pressure check that the company does not offer by mail. Her supervisor later said the pressure drops below the threshold only in older homes, which my house is not. I have a water test from the county showing lead well below the action level, and I want to know why the unit could not hold up to it.

Here is what I want. I am asking for a full refund of the 389 dollar unit price and the two cartridges, and a prepaid label to send the housing back. I will ask Kelsey to note on the account that I did not receive the pressure check. If the company says no, I will take it to my card issuer for a dispute, and I will keep the box, the receipts, and the test results. I expect this to get resolved within two weeks, and I would rather not have to write a second letter.

On May 9 I ordered a three tier birthday cake from Maple and Ember Bakehouse for my mother's seventieth. I asked for a chocolate sponge, a salted caramel filling, and a fudge frosting on the outside, and I sent a photo of the design I wanted. The woman who took the order, Corrine, read it back to me on the phone and said it would be ready by noon on Saturday. I paid 186 dollars and picked a pickup slot for eleven.

When I opened the box at the party, the top tier had slid to one side and the frosting had cracked along the seam. The sponge was dry, and the filling was not salted at all. It tasted like plain caramel, and the fudge outside was more like glaze, a thin, sweet shell that cracked when we cut the slices. The caramel sauce had separated into a greasy layer on top. Two of my aunts asked if it came from the grocery store. My mother was gracious about it, but I could tell she was disappointed, and I was embarrassed in front of people who had traveled three hours for the party.

I called the shop on Monday and left a message. Corrine called back on Wednesday, apologized, and offered a 20 dollar credit toward my next order. I turned it down and asked for a full refund, since the cake was not what I paid for. She said a manager would review it and get back to me within five business days. That was three weeks ago. I have not heard from anyone, and the credit has not appeared. I want the full 186 dollars returned to my card, and I want a written explanation of how the cake went out the door in that condition.

I dropped my Corvane gravel bike off at Spokeline Cycle on April 2 for a tune up and a new chain. The front desk guy, Jarek, wrote the ticket and told me it would be ready Thursday. It is now the following Tuesday, and the bike is still sitting on a stand in the back. Every time I call, someone says the mechanic is examining the bottom bracket, and nobody can tell me what that means or what it will cost.

The first time I went in to see it, the bike was on the floor with the wheels off and a tag on the handlebars that said parts pending. Jarek admitted the shop had ordered the wrong size chain and had to wait a week for the right one. Fair enough. But the new chain went on at the second visit, and the derailleur was still out of adjustment. When I rode it home, the chain skipped on the big cog every time I climbed a hill. I have sent the bike back once already, and I still do not trust the shifting.

I will need a clear estimate before anything else gets touched. I expect the shop to put the bottom bracket work in writing, with a price and a date, and I expect them to stop the work if the cost climbs past the quote. If they hand me another bill with a vague line about labor, I will ask for the old parts back and take my business elsewhere. I know the warnings on my last bill were all about wear, but that is no excuse for a repair that never got finished. Next week I will bring the bike in myself and watch the adjustment.
